# Preface {.unnumbered}

## What this book is

There are good textbooks on databases. There is no textbook on a single
modern stream processing engine.

Garcia-Molina, Ullman and Widom's *Database Systems: The Complete Book*
will teach you relational algebra, SQL, B-trees and the canonical query
optimizer. Petrov's *Database Internals* will guide you through storage
engines and distributed consensus. Kleppmann's *Designing Data-Intensive
Applications* will give you the conceptual map of the data-systems
landscape, batch and stream alike. None of them takes a single
streaming system, opens it up, and walks you through what is actually
inside.

This book does that, using NebulaStream as the specimen. NebulaStream
is an end-to-end data-management system for cloud-edge-sensor
deployments, developed jointly at BIFOLD by the DIMA Group at TU Berlin
and the DFKI IAM Group. It is written in C++23, generates native code
for every query through a custom JIT framework called Nautilus, and is
designed from the ground up to run across the full sensor-fog-cloud
spectrum.

We will not pretend NebulaStream is the only or best stream processing
engine. We chose it because it is small enough to be tractable, large
enough to be interesting, and unusually well-documented in tree. The
techniques you will see — code generation, watermarks, two-queue
schedulers, plugin registries — appear in Flink, in Materialize, in
Arroyo, in Hyper. NebulaStream is the worked example. The lessons
generalize.

## What this book is not

It is not a user manual. If you want to learn how to write a SELECT
statement against NebulaStream, the official documentation will serve
you better.

It is not a comparative survey. Tyler Akidau, Slava Chernyak and Reuven
Lax wrote *Streaming Systems* for that. We will compare to other
engines in short, well-bounded sidebars when the comparison illuminates
a NebulaStream design choice, and not otherwise.

It is not a course in distributed systems theory. We assume you know
why a leader election matters, what linearizability is, and why
networks partition. Where NebulaStream's design depends on a particular
theoretical result, we cite the paper and move on.

## How to read it

The book is organised into five parts.

**Part I: Foundations** establishes the vocabulary. You will see how a
SQL query becomes native code in roughly forty pages. The remaining
twenty-one chapters fill in the steps.

**Part II: The Query Frontier** covers the path from text to a logical
plan: parser, algebra, time and watermarks, sources and sinks.

**Part III: Optimization and Compilation** covers the path from a
logical plan to executable native code: rule-based optimizer, physical
lowering, pipelining, JIT code generation.

**Part IV: Runtime and Execution** covers what happens when the
generated code starts processing tuples: task scheduling, state
management, error handling, the worker process.

**Part V: Operations and Frontiers** covers everything around the engine:
distributed deployment, testing, benchmarking, open research problems.

Most chapters depend on Part I but are otherwise reasonably
independent. If you are interested in code generation, jump to Chapter
12. If you are interested in scheduling, jump to Chapter 15. The full
chapter graph is in @sec-dependencies.

## Conventions

Throughout the book we use four kinds of callout boxes.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 0.1: Anatomy of a callout"}
**Examples** ground abstract definitions in concrete, runnable scenarios.
They appear every few pages.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how this differs in Flink"}
**Real-system references** are short comparative sidebars, never longer
than half a page. They place a NebulaStream design choice in the wider
landscape.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 0.1"}
**Reading exercises** point you at a real test in `nes-systests/`. Run
it, observe what happens, then come back. There are no problem-set-style
exercises in this edition; a separate companion volume contains those.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Caveat"}
**Caveats** flag where the live code differs from a published design
document, where a feature is partially implemented, or where the
authors disagree about the right approach.
:::

File paths are written in `monospace` and refer to a specific
commit-pinned snapshot of NebulaStream. The pinned commit is recorded
on the copyright page. Code listings name their source file and line
range. If the file or range no longer resolves, the book's continuous
integration job will warn before the next edition ships.

## A note on currency

NebulaStream is an actively developed engine. The codebase
moves; design documents do not. An earlier revision of this
manuscript anchored several chapters on the in-tree
`docs/design/` documents — which are dated 2024 — as if they
described 2026 reality. They do not. The implementation has
evolved significantly past several of those design documents,
most visibly in the distribution layer (Chapter 19), where what
was research roadmap in 2024 is the production data plane in
2026.

Chapter 19 has been rewritten to reflect this; smaller
adjustments appear in Chapters 1, 2, 13, 14, 16, 18, and 22.
The rule we have settled on for the rest of the manuscript:
**design documents are historical context; the live code is
authoritative.** Where we cite a design document, we cite it for
the rationale it captures, not as a description of current
state. The book's `scripts/drift-check.py` verifies that file
paths and line ranges still resolve, but it cannot verify that
*narratives* still match behaviour. That part requires
maintainer review.
